chunks.title: The succession to Stalin, 1953–1957
chunks.body:
When Stalin died in March 1953, power passed to a "collective leadership". **Georgii Malenkov** became head of government, **Lavrentii Beria** kept the secret police, and **Nikita Khrushchev**, by no means the best-known of Stalin's heirs, was a party secretary. Beria moved fastest to change policy: he repudiated the Doctors' Plot and backed the release of prisoners. Fearing his power, Khrushchev conspired with Malenkov and others to have Beria arrested on 26 June 1953; he was secretly tried and shot in December. Khrushchev was confirmed as First Secretary.

Malenkov's "New Course" promised more consumer goods. Khrushchev countered with the **Virgin Lands** scheme and built alliances with Mikoian, Bulganin and Marshal Zhukov, and in February 1955 Malenkov was forced out as prime minister. As Lewis Siegelbaum puts it, Khrushchev won "by reviving the party apparatus and reasserting its control" over the state.

In 1957 he faced his greatest challenge. After he broke up the central industrial ministries into 107 regional economic councils, Molotov, Kaganovich and other Stalinists tried to remove him in the Presidium. Khrushchev appealed to the full Central Committee; with Zhukov's help in flying in his supporters, it denounced his opponents as an "**anti-Party group**". The losers were demoted, not shot, and Zhukov himself was retired in October.

This mattered because Khrushchev rose through the party apparatus, as Stalin had, but after Beria without killing his rivals, which meant that defeated opponents lost their posts rather than their lives.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Beria's removal decided the first round.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Beria had been the boldest reformer.

The anti-Party group crisis confirmed his power.

chunks.title: De-Stalinisation and its limits
chunks.body:
The new leaders could not rule as Stalin had. An amnesty in March 1953 freed over 1.5 million prisoners within three months, revolts broke out in camps such as Norilsk and Vorkuta, and between 1953 and 1956 some five million prisoners left the Gulag.

In February 1956, at a closed session of the **Twentieth Party Congress**, Khrushchev delivered his "**Secret Speech**". He detailed the arrest and execution of loyal communists in the 1930s, the unpreparedness of 1941, wartime blunders and the deportation of whole peoples, and blamed Stalin's "cult of personality". But he said nothing of collectivisation and the famine, and nothing of the responsibility of other leaders, including himself. Judt warns that the speech's significance "should not be overstated": Khrushchev was a true believer who blamed Stalin in order to save the Leninist system and his own generation.

The speech shook the communist world. In Poland workers demonstrated at Poznań, and in October 1956 a revolution broke out in Hungary. When Imre Nagy announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, Soviet troops attacked Budapest on 4 November; as many as 200,000 Hungarians fled and Nagy was executed in 1958.

At home the **Thaw** brought cautious cultural freedom. In 1962 Solzhenitsyn's account of a labour camp, *One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich*, was published. Yet Khrushchev also defended socialist realism, crudely attacked abstract art at the Manege exhibition in 1962, and allowed no direct criticism of the leadership.

This mattered because de-Stalinisation ended mass terror without ending the party's monopoly, which meant that reform was always limited by the need to protect the system Stalin had built.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Secret Speech broke with Stalin's cult.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It protected Lenin and the party.

chunks.title: Agriculture, welfare and the economy
chunks.body:
Khrushchev's great passion was agriculture. His **Virgin Lands** campaign ploughed 19 million hectares of steppe in Kazakhstan and Siberia in 1954 and 14 million more in 1955. In 1956 the harvest was the largest in Soviet history, with more than half its grain from the new lands. But single-crop farming exhausted the soil: Judt reports half a million tons of topsoil washing away each year. His **corn campaign** expanded maize to 37 million hectares by 1962, much of it in unsuitable climates, and in the cool, wet year of 1962 most of the crop died. After the disastrous harvest of 1963, the USSR had to import grain from the West. Meanwhile the tiny private plots, 3 per cent of the land, produced over a third of agricultural output.

In welfare, Khrushchev's record was better. In 1956 the 1940 law that made leaving a job a crime was abolished; a minimum wage, a shorter working day, maternity leave and a national pension scheme followed. Housing became a priority: in 1956–60 it took 23.5 per cent of all investment, and millions moved into cheap prefabricated blocks, mocked as *khrushcheby*. But the 1961 promise to end the housing shortage within a decade was not kept.

The economy remained fragile. When meat and dairy prices were raised in 1962, workers at **Novocherkassk** protested; troops opened fire on 2 June, killing twenty-four people, and seven protesters were later executed.

This mattered because Khrushchev raised living standards but failed to fix agriculture, which meant that his promises of plenty made his failures more visible.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Virgin Lands brought brief success.

chunks.title: Prestige abroad and the fall of 1964
chunks.body:
Khrushchev wanted "peaceful coexistence" with the West. In 1955 he agreed the Austrian State Treaty and visited Tito's Yugoslavia to repair relations. Soviet science gave him propaganda triumphs: **Sputnik**, the first artificial satellite, was launched on 4 October 1957, and on 12 April 1961 **Iurii Gagarin** became the first man in space. But Khrushchev's boasts of missile strength were empty: by September 1961 US intelligence estimated that the Soviet Union had no more than twenty-five intercontinental missiles. The Twenty-Second Party Congress of October 1961 revealed a deep split with China.

By 1964 his colleagues had lost patience. Agricultural failure, grain imports, the shock of Novocherkassk and his reorganisation of economic administration had alienated them. In the Kremlin coup of **October 1964**, Judt writes, the plotters were irritated by his policy failures and his autocratic style, but above all by his inconsistencies: others might misread his unpredictable tolerance. Khrushchev was removed from office; he lived until 1971.

This mattered because Khrushchev was removed by his colleagues and lived on until 1971, which meant that his fall was itself evidence of how far the Soviet system had changed since Stalin.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Foreign policy mixed coexistence with crisis.
Failures and inconsistency led to his removal.

useItInAnEssay.prove: After the disastrous 1963 harvest the USSR imported grain by January 1964, and Judt writes that the plotters of October 1964 were irritated by his policy failures, autocratic style and inconsistencies.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the party leadership saw him as a risk to stability, so it used its power to remove him.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the fact that he was removed and lived until 1971 showed that the system he had reformed no longer killed defeated leaders.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Khrushchev therefore fell because of his failures, in a manner that reflected his own reforms.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the successes and failures of Khrushchev's domestic and foreign policies between 1953 and 1964.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout

modelPlan.thesis: In both spheres Khrushchev combined bold initiatives with failures: at home, de-Stalinisation and welfare against agricultural collapse; abroad, peaceful coexistence and space triumphs against Hungary, empty missile boasts and the split with China.
modelPlan.counter: His space triumphs were domestic propaganda successes as well as foreign ones.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Where did he succeed more? At home in humanising the system; abroad in prestige rather than power.

segments.text: Khrushchev's record was mixed in both spheres, but his domestic successes were more lasting.
At home some five million left the Gulag and pensions and a minimum wage were introduced, whereas abroad Sputnik and Gagarin brought prestige that his missile boasts could not back up.
This meant that his domestic reforms changed how the system treated its citizens, while his foreign successes were largely symbolic.
However, both spheres also brought failures: grain imports and Novocherkassk at home, the crushing of Hungary and the split with China abroad.
His domestic policy was therefore the more successful, because its reforms outlasted him.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why Khrushchev was removed from power between 1962 and 1964.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Khrushchev was removed because agricultural failure, unrest over prices and grain imports discredited his promises, while his autocratic style and unpredictability alarmed the colleagues whose support he depended on.
modelPlan.counter: That he was removed and lived until 1971 was itself a product of his own reforms.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? His inconsistency, which turned failures into a threat to his colleagues.

segments.text: Khrushchev was removed because his failures and unpredictability made him a liability to the party leadership.
In 1962 most of the corn crop died and troops fired on protesters at Novocherkassk, and after the 1963 harvest the USSR imported grain by January 1964.
This meant that his promises of plenty had visibly failed, so his colleagues could blame him for shortages and unrest.
However, Judt stresses that above all the plotters were uneasy at his inconsistencies, as his unpredictable tolerance might be misread.
Khrushchev was therefore removed because failure and inconsistency together convinced the leadership that he threatened the system's stability.
